title: Planet Earth: Shape, Structure and Atmosphere
description: Earth as an oblate spheroid — interior structure, atmosphere and observing conditions.
content_html:
Earth’s True Shape

When you look at a globe it appears to be a perfect sphere, but the real Earth is subtly flattened. It is an oblate spheroid — a sphere that bulges at the equator and is slightly squashed at the poles. This equatorial bulge exists because the spinning Earth throws material outward along its widest girth. The mean diameter of the Earth is approximately 13 000 km, but the equatorial diameter is about 43 km greater than the polar diameter. For most astronomical calculations we treat Earth as a perfect sphere, but the difference matters when calculating precise coordinates.

Key Fact

Earth has a mean diameter of approximately 13 000 km and is an oblate spheroid — slightly wider at the equator than at the poles due to its rotation.

Earth’s Internal Structure

Earth is layered like an onion. At the surface is the crust, which is the thin rocky skin we live on. Beneath it lies the mantle — a thick layer of semi-molten rock that flows very slowly over millions of years. Deeper still is the outer core, a liquid layer of iron and nickel whose motion generates Earth’s magnetic field. At the very centre is the inner core, a solid ball of iron and nickel compressed by immense pressure. This internal structure is relevant to astronomy because the liquid outer core produces the magnetosphere — Earth’s protective magnetic bubble that deflects harmful charged particles from the Sun.

Solar wind — a continuous stream of charged particles from the Sun — would strip away Earth’s atmosphere if the magnetosphere did not deflect it. The magnetosphere is not symmetrical: the solar wind compresses it on the dayside and stretches it into a long magnetotail on the night-side. This asymmetric teardrop shape is the correct one to draw in exam answers. Where solar wind particles do penetrate at the poles, they excite atmospheric gases to produce the aurora borealis (Northern Lights) and aurora australis (Southern Lights) — phenomena that no telescope is needed to appreciate.

Latitude and Longitude

To locate any point on Earth’s surface we use two angular coordinates. Latitude measures how far north or south of the Equator (0°) a place lies, reaching 90° at each pole. Longitude measures how far east or west of the Prime Meridian (0°) a place lies, reaching 180° in either direction. The Prime Meridian passes through Greenwich, London. Together, a latitude and longitude pair pinpoints any location on Earth.

Several parallels of latitude have special names. The Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N) is the most northerly latitude at which the Sun can be directly overhead at noon, which it is at the June solstice. The Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S) is the equivalent in the Southern Hemisphere, where the Sun is overhead at the December solstice. The Arctic Circle (66.5° N) marks the boundary north of which the Sun can remain above or below the horizon for a full 24 hours around the solstices. The Antarctic Circle (66.5° S) is the Southern Hemisphere equivalent. Both latitude values — 23.5° and 66.5° — come directly from Earth’s axial tilt of 23.5°.

Key Fact

Five named parallels: Equator (0°), Tropic of Cancer (23.5° N), Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° S), Arctic Circle (66.5° N) and Antarctic Circle (66.5° S). The 23.5° and 66.5° values both arise from Earth’s axial tilt.

Earth’s Atmosphere and the Astronomer

The atmosphere is both a friend and an enemy to the ground-based astronomer. On the plus side, it filters out much of the harmful ultraviolet and X-ray radiation from space. On the minus side, it introduces several problems for observers.

The most familiar effect is the blue colour of the daytime sky. Sunlight contains all wavelengths, but the atmosphere scatters shorter (blue) wavelengths far more efficiently than longer (red) wavelengths — a phenomenon called Rayleigh scattering. Blue light bounces around the sky in every direction, making the sky appear blue. At sunset and sunrise the Sun is low and its light travels through a much thicker slice of atmosphere, scattering away nearly all the blue and leaving warm reds and oranges. This has no practical effect on night-time observing, but it does explain why Venus and Mercury are easiest to spot just after sunset or before sunrise, when the sky colour is still shifting.

Atmospheric seeing is the blurring caused by turbulent air. Different air pockets at different temperatures act like tiny lenses, bending the light path and making stellar images shimmer and blur. Professional observatories use a measure called the seeing disc (in arcseconds) to quantify this — a smaller number is better. From the UK, typical seeing is 1–3 arcseconds, but on a still night with stable air, it can drop below 1 arcsecond, revealing fine planetary detail. The twinkling of stars is the same effect noticed by the naked eye: the scintillation of point sources caused by atmospheric turbulence. Planets appear less prone to twinkling because they are extended discs, so random fluctuations average out.

Skyglow is the orange or white haze visible above towns at night. Streetlights, car headlights and illuminated buildings scatter artificial light upward into the atmosphere, where it reflects back and raises the background brightness of the sky. This washes out faint objects. The Bortle scale (1–9) measures sky darkness: Class 1 is a pristine dark-sky site where the Milky Way casts a shadow; Class 9 is an inner-city sky where only the Moon and brightest stars and planets are visible.

The naked-eye limiting magnitude — the faintest star visible without optical aid — varies dramatically with light pollution: approximately magnitude 6 under a dark sky (Bortle 1–2), around magnitude 4 in suburban areas (Bortle 5–6), and as poor as magnitude 2 in city centres (Bortle 8–9). Planning a naked-eye observation session should always include checking your Bortle class or using a smartphone app to assess sky darkness before travelling to a site.
exam_tip_html: When drawing the Earth’s magnetosphere in exam answers, always draw an asymmetric shape: compressed on the Sun-facing side and drawn out into a long magnetotail on the night-side. A symmetric bubble shape will lose marks. For questions about the named parallels of latitude, remember that the Tropic angles (23.5°) match Earth’s axial tilt and the Arctic/Antarctic Circle angles (66.5°) are the complement (90° − 23.5°). For 3-mark explain questions about atmospheric seeing or sky colour, link cause (turbulent air pockets / Rayleigh scattering), mechanism (bending of light / scattering of short wavelengths) and effect (blurring / blue sky) — one statement per mark.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Earth is an oblate spheroid with a mean diameter of ~13 000 km, layered from crust to inner core. The liquid outer core generates the magnetosphere, which has an asymmetric teardrop shape due to the solar wind.
  • Latitude and longitude locate any point on Earth. The five named parallels — Equator (0°), Tropics (23.5°), Arctic and Antarctic Circles (66.5°) — all arise from Earth’s 23.5° axial tilt.
  • The atmosphere causes sky colour (Rayleigh scattering), atmospheric seeing (turbulence), twinkling of stars (scintillation) and skyglow (artificial light pollution). Naked-eye limiting magnitude ranges from magnitude 6 in dark skies to magnitude 2 in city centres.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the shape of the Earth?
A) A perfect sphere
B) An oblate spheroid
C) A prolate spheroid
D) A flat disc
State the approximate mean diameter of the Earth.
Name the two outermost layers of Earth, starting from the surface.

The Brackenfell Observing Society is planning a night of naked-eye observation from a suburban back garden. A member notes that only stars brighter than about magnitude 4 are visible. Explain why this is the case and describe one action the group could take to improve their limiting magnitude.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correctly identifies skyglow / light pollution as the cause [1]; explains that artificial light is scattered by the atmosphere raising the background sky brightness, which masks faint stars [1]; suggests a practical action such as travelling to a darker site / using a Bortle Class 1-3 location / using a red-light torch and allowing at least 20 minutes for dark adaptation [1].
Secure: Identifies light pollution and gives explanation or action but not all three elements.
Developing: Names light pollution but explanation is vague.
Emerging: Response is too brief or incorrect.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the sky appears blue during the day but reddish-orange at sunrise and sunset.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: States that shorter wavelengths (blue light) are scattered more strongly than longer wavelengths (red/orange) by the atmosphere [1]; during the day sunlight reaches the eye from all directions as scattered blue light, making the sky appear blue [1]; at sunrise/sunset light travels through a much thicker layer of atmosphere so nearly all blue light is scattered away, leaving predominantly red and orange wavelengths [1].
Secure: Two of the three marking points correctly linked.
Developing: Mentions scattering but does not distinguish wavelengths or path length.
Emerging: Vague or incorrect.

practice_questions.text:
Dr Halima Yousef is explaining the difference between atmospheric seeing and twinkling (scintillation) to a group of students at a planetarium. Compare these two phenomena, including their causes and the types of astronomical object most affected by each.

Your answer should include a discussion of at least two points of comparison.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Accurate description of atmospheric seeing as blurring caused by turbulent air pockets bending the light path, quantified by the seeing disc in arcseconds; smaller values indicate better seeing. Accurate description of twinkling (scintillation) as the rapid shimmer of point sources caused by the same atmospheric turbulence. Key comparison: both have the same root cause (atmospheric turbulence) but seeing is a measure used by telescopic observers to assess image quality, while twinkling is the naked-eye experience of the same effect. Stars are point sources so they twinkle more readily; planets are extended discs so random fluctuations average out, making them less prone to twinkling. Candidate may note that professional observatories are sited above much of the turbulent atmosphere (high altitude) to minimise both effects.
Secure (3-4): Correct cause for at least one phenomenon and at least one valid comparison point.
Developing (1-2): One or two relevant facts but lacks comparison.
Emerging (0): No credit-worthy content.

flashcard_questions.q: What shape is the Earth, and why is it not a perfect sphere?
flashcard_questions.a: An oblate spheroid — rotation causes an equatorial bulge and slight polar flattening.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the approximate mean diameter of the Earth?
Name Earth's four internal layers from the surface inward.
flashcard_questions.a: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core.

flashcard_questions.q: Which layer of Earth generates the magnetosphere, and why?
flashcard_questions.a: The liquid outer core — motion of molten iron and nickel creates a magnetic field.
A 1-to-9 scale measuring sky darkness: 1 is pristine dark sky, 9 is inner-city sky.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the naked-eye limiting magnitude in a dark sky, suburban sky and city?
flashcard_questions.a: Dark sky: magnitude 6; suburban: magnitude 4; city: magnitude 2.
Blurring of telescope images caused by turbulent air pockets bending starlight.

flashcard_questions.q: Why do stars twinkle but planets generally do not?
flashcard_questions.a: Stars are point sources so turbulence causes scintillation; planets are extended discs so fluctuations average out.
The diffuse glow above a settlement caused by artificial light scattered back by the atmosphere.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is the daytime sky blue?
flashcard_questions.a: Rayleigh scattering — shorter blue wavelengths scatter more strongly than red wavelengths in all directions.

flashcard_questions.q: At what latitude does the Sun reach the zenith at noon on the June solstice?
What does the Arctic Circle (66.5° N) mark?
flashcard_questions.a: The boundary north of which the Sun can stay above or below the horizon for a full 24 hours.

flashcard_questions.q: Where is the Prime Meridian (0° longitude) located?

glossary_terms.definition: A sphere squashed slightly at the poles and bulging slightly at the equator due to the planet's rotation.
Earth's thin, solid outermost rocky layer, ranging from about 5 km thick under oceans to 70 km under mountain ranges.
The region of space around Earth dominated by its magnetic field, shielding the surface from solar wind particles.
Angular distance measured north or south of the Equator, from 0° at the Equator to 90° at the poles.
Distortion and blurring of starlight caused by turbulent pockets of air at different temperatures moving across the line of sight.
The diffuse glow above a town or city caused by artificial light reflected and scattered back down by the atmosphere.
A nine-level numerical scale measuring the darkness of the night sky, from Class 1 (pristine dark site) to Class 9 (inner-city sky).
The scattering of light by molecules in the atmosphere, affecting shorter wavelengths (blue) much more strongly than longer wavelengths (red).
